----------------------------------------



Most knowledge work still starts with an act of translation. You finish a customer call and turn it into a bug report. You think through a story idea on a walk, then wait until you’re back at your laptop to organize it. Before the real work can begin, you’ve already spent time cleaning up the context.

Paired with an AI agent, voice can remove that intermediate step. You can speak while the details are fresh https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIERlZmluaXRpdmUgR3VpZGUgdG8gVXNpbmcgVm9pY2UgV2l0aCBBSSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzOTUsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL3d3dy5tb25vbG9ndWUudG8iLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6OH0=, point the agent toward the relevant transcripts, code, documents, or messages, define the outcome you want, and review what it produces.

A useful way to start is with a five-step loop:

Capture → retrieve and ground → define the outcome → act → review and redirect

Today we’re publishing “Build Faster With Voice,” https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGhlIERlZmluaXRpdmUgR3VpZGUgdG8gVXNpbmcgVm9pY2UgV2l0aCBBSSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzOTUsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL2d1aWRlcy9idWlsZC1mYXN0ZXItd2l0aC12b2ljZSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo5fQ== a practical guide to using that loop across writing, planning, software, communication, and ongoing memory systems.

The full guide is available to paid and All Access Every members. It includes:

 * More than a dozen workflows based on how people at Every use voice with agents
 * Copyable prompts for turning recordings into article outlines, project plans, bug patches, emails, meeting follow-ups, and more
 * Setup instructions for connecting your notes and transcripts to Codex or Claude
 * The context, safeguards, and review steps each workflow needs

If you’re reading Every for free, the five-step loop above is yours to try. To get the complete prompts, setup instructions, and workflow library, you’ll need to upgrade to a paid Every subscription.

Voice doesn’t eliminate the need for good sources or careful review. Agents still need access to the material that has the final say, and consequential actions should still require your approval. The advantage is that you no longer have to turn every messy thought into polished instructions before the work can start.

INSIDE EVERY

MAKING SLACK AGENT-NATIVE

If you’ve been following our coverage, you know that many people at Every—CEO Dan Shipper https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiV2hhdCBJZiBTbGFjayBXYXMgWW91ciBBSSBDb21tYW5kIENlbnRlciIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNjAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BkYW5zaGlwcGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjZ9, head of growth Austin Tedesco https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiV2hhdCBJZiBTbGFjayBXYXMgWW91ciBBSSBDb21tYW5kIENlbnRlciIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNjAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0B0ZWRlc2NhdSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo3fQ==, and head of operations Arielle Shipper, to name a few—have reduced the mental fragmentation of bouncing between apps by working almost exclusively within Codex https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiV2hhdCBJZiBTbGFjayBXYXMgWW91ciBBSSBDb21tYW5kIENlbnRlciIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNjAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL2NvbnRleHQtd2luZG93L2NvZGV4LWluLXByYWN0aWNlIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjh9. It’s where they handle emails, write Slack messages, build new features, and draft articles using Codex’s in-app browser.

Senior applied AI engineer Nityesh Agarwal https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiV2hhdCBJZiBTbGFjayBXYXMgWW91ciBBSSBDb21tYW5kIENlbnRlciIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNjAsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BuaXR5ZXNoIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjl9 is a fan of the general concept but thinks there’s a better, model-agnostic platform for AI-assisted work: Slack, which is optimized to make it easy to manage multiple tasks at once and reduce context-switching.

Here’s how he turned the platform into an agent-native operating system

Nityesh first created a personal Slack coding agent—named Luo Ji, after the protagonist in science fiction series The Three-Body Problem. Slack has long allowed developers to create bots and apps on its platform and connect them to outside servers. Using that infrastructure, Nityesh connected Luo Ji to Claude Code https://every. on a spare Macbook Air, which functions as a server.

Then he modified the connector script to meet his specifications, including a routing rule: Each top-level message in a Slack channel kicks off a new Claude Code session, while a reply in the resulting message thread resumes that same session. (He used the same general setup to build Claudie https://every., the consulting team’s AI project manager.)

https://every. long-running Slack thread between Nityesh and Luo Ji. (Screenshot courtesy of Nityesh Agarwal.)




With this in place, Slack becomes a full-blown project management tool. Nityesh keeps a channel for each project, and each conversation thread within that project channel is an individual task. When Luo Ji completes a task, it sends Nityesh a notification and marks the thread unread, letting him know that there’s completed work to review.

Since Slack allows file attachments, Luo Ji can post screenshots of what it built to make the review even easier. Nityesh can request a change, or mark the thread unread and come back to it later. The chat history remains attached to the task instead of getting buried in a long agent conversation or scattered across tabs, turning the platform into a project dashboard.

This is a free preview of a subscribers-only post.

On Friday, we published our Vibe Check of Claude Opus 5 https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by92aWJlLWNoZWNrL29wdXMtNSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo1fQ==. A small group of us had spent the week testing it, and we found a model that was brilliant in flashes and frustrating in practice. Then the rest of the Every team got their hands on it.

Their experiences over the weekend confirmed the model’s unruliness—and suggested a way to tame it. We also have the second essay in our series in partnership with Maven on “unlearning,” a workflow for checking whether skills built for an older model are getting in the new one’s way, and a theory as to why one-shot AI demos of video games clog your social feeds.

PULSE CHECK

GETTING THROWN BY OPUS 5

Toward the end of Every’s all-team standup on Monday, the conversation turned to Opus 5. More people from the team had tried it by then, and the same quirks kept coming up.

Head of operations Arielle Shipper found that Opus 5 needed too much management and repeated prompting to keep its responses simple—more than Fable or Opus 4.8. Cora https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9jb3JhLmNvbXB1dGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjd9 general manager Kieran Klaassen https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9Aa2llcmFuXzEzNTUiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6OH0= advanced a theory that the new Opus is intended to be a subagent to Fable, and communicates as though it were speaking to agents instead of humans.

It was also prickly; during a decluttering project, Opus successfully inventoried head of consulting Natalia Quintero https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AbmF0YWxpYV8yOTQ0IiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjl9’s belongings and planned donations, but adopted an irritating, judgmental tone, criticizing her for owning 15 water bottles. Senior editor Jack Cheng https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AamFja2NoZW5nIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjEwfQ== shared a screenshot of Opus backhandedly calling one of his comments the most interesting thing he had said all session. Software engineer Kai Zau thought Anthropic had dialed up the model’s disagreeableness, while fellow engineer Lee Knowlton joked that Opus 6 might finally tell users they had said something insightful.

Prickliness aside, the team converged toward a specific way of working with the new Opus model. CEO Dan Shipper https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AZGFuc2hpcHBlciIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjoxMX0= and Spiral https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93cml0ZXRoZXNwaXJhbC5jb20iLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6MTJ9 general manager Marcus Moretti https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVGFtaW5nIE9wdXMgNSIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQzNTksInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AbWFyY3VzX2ZkODMwMl8xIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjEzfQ== had both handed Opus a substantial job with a clear finish line, then left it alone. Jack told it he was about to step away from the computer, and to batch its work and ask any blocking questions. All three got good results. Anthropic’s prompting guide https://every. makes the same recommendation: Put the full brief in the first prompt and let Opus run.

Software development is about to change in ways many teams outside the frontier labs haven’t had to think about yet. Our new interactive piece, “Before the Deluge,” shows what that looks like from the inside.

We spoke with six members of OpenAI’s infrastructure team—including its vice president of applied infrastructure engineering—about three converging pressures: an overwhelming surge of AI-generated code, software-development infrastructure pushed to its limits, and a fundamental redesign of how code gets reviewed and kept reliable.

What they’re working through now is a preview of what’s coming for software development everywhere.

“Before the Deluge” reveals how those pressures interact, what the engineers are doing to hold the system together, and what the broader software community will need to reckon with as AI-generated code becomes routine. ## [GPT-5.6 vs Claude, benchmarked on real agent work](https://ref.viktor.com/vik-aiv-main6-post)

Viktor is the AI employee that 50,000+ teams run inside Slack and Microsoft Teams, so when OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6 we benchmarked Sol, Terra, and Luna against Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 on real agent work: actual tasks inside simulated company workspaces, graded on outcomes.

What we found: Sol ties Fable 5 on quality at 76%, at a third of the cost ($33.55 vs $96.35 per run). The cost-performance frontier is entirely OpenAI. GPT-5.6 finishes a median task in 66 to 82 seconds, Claude needs 129 to 151.
